newsitem.title: USA: Oil tanker fixed, OK'd for loading and transit.
newsitem.headline: Oil tanker fixed, OK'd for loading and transit.

text.p: A Chevron oil tanker that was hit by steering troubles Tuesday has been repaired, inspected and cleared by the U.S. Coast Guard to leave the port with its load of crude oil, a company spokesman said Wednesday.

The Chevron Mississippi, which had been escorted into Alaska's Prince William Sound by three tugs, was scheduled to depart the Valdez port with its cargo on Thursday, said Dean O'Hair, a Seattle-based public-affairs manager for Chevron.
The electrical fault that caused the problem with the main steering system was repaired, O'Hair said.
He characterized the problem as minor, one that was detected during a "routine pre-arrival test" conducted before the ship entered Prince William Sound.
The ship used its backup steering system to dock Tuesday at the Valdez marine terminal of the trans-Alaska pipeline.

During its voyage to Valdez, the Chevron Mississippi contained no crude oil, the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) said. But DEC said it was concerned about the ship's supply of bunker oil used as fuel.
The escort tug system in Prince William Sound was imposed by state and federal laws after the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill.
The policy of providing escort tugs for tanker vessels arriving at the Valdez port was instituted later, in 1994, partly in response to concerns about floating glacier ice in transit lanes.

The trans-Alaska pipeline, owned by seven oil companies with interests on Alaska's North Slope, carries an average of 1.4 million to 1.5 million barrels of oil a day, according to state and industry figures.
